title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
authors: Jordan Hoffmann, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch (equal contribution), Elena Buchatskaya, Trevor Cai, Eliza Rutherford, Diego de Las Casas, Lisa Anne Hendricks, Johannes Welbl, Aidan Clark, Tom Hennigan, Eric Noland, Katie Millican, George van den Driessche, Bogdan Damoc, Aurelia Guy, Simon Osindero, Karen Simonyan, Erich Elsen, Jack W. Rae, Oriol Vinyals, Laurent Sifre

code.title: no official release; Epoch AI's replication data
code.note: the paper released no code, data or model. Besiroglu et al. (2024) recovered 245 final losses from the vector graphics of Figure 4 and published them with their refitting notebook (no licence file); this page's Refit tab runs on those points

takeaway: Compute-optimal training scales params and tokens equally (about 20 tokens/param); a 70B model on 1.4T tokens beat Gopher 280B at the same FLOPs, and modern practice deliberately overtrains past this point for cheaper inference.
verdict: Believe the allocation: parameters and tokens should grow together, about 20 tokens per parameter at these scales. Two independent methods in the paper agree, the 70B-against-280B test confirms it, and every replication since lands near 0.5 (Approach 2 on points read off the paper's own figure gives 0.51 here). Do not reuse the Approach 3 constants (E 1.69, A 406.4, B 410.7, α 0.34, β 0.28) or its intervals: the optimiser stopped early, and a correct fit gives a different law. The benchmark wins come from one pair of runs, with no seeds.

resources.n: the best conceptual unpacking of what the result means; reframes scaling as data-bound rather than parameter-bound and works through the loss equation term by term.

resources.t: Chinchilla data-optimal scaling laws: in plain English
resources.n: the 20-tokens-per-parameter heuristic spelled out, with tables applying it to real model sizes.

refits Approach 3 from data read off the paper's Figure 4, finds the fitting problems, and shows the corrected fit agrees with Approaches 1 and 2. The essential critique; the arXiv version is 2404.10102.

resources.t: Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws
resources.n: extends the scaling law to include inference cost, formalising why everyone now overtrains past the Chinchilla point; trains 47 models up to 10,000 tokens per parameter.

resources.t: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models
resources.n: explains the Kaplan against Chinchilla gap cause by cause (output-layer FLOPs, warmup, optimiser tuning) and finds that matching the cosine schedule, this paper's explanation, matters little.
modern end-to-end treatment of the scaling-law literature, from Kaplan through Chinchilla to current practice, with the fitting pitfalls spelled out.

kb.t: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (Kaplan et al.)
kb.n: 2020: the result this paper corrects. Its Then-and-now tab animates both allocation rules spending the same budgets, and its toy sweep shows why a small CPU sweep cannot find the optimum.
2020: the archetypal under-trained model by this paper's account (175B on 300B tokens; Table 3 says 3.7T).
2024: fits its own IsoFLOP law to choose 405B, and deliberately overtrains the 8B and 70B models for inference economics.
2024: modern frontier practice, a heavily overtrained mixture of experts (14.8T tokens, 37B active parameters); MoE needs its own scaling treatment.
2021: sparse models change the N in the FLOP accounting; this paper's related work flags that MoE scaling analyses shared Kaplan's fixed-token-count flaw.
2024: an open sparse model whose active and total parameters differ, the case Chinchilla's dense law does not cover.
2025: decay-free learning-rate schedules with checkpoint merging, one answer to the schedule-length problem this paper raised against Kaplan.
2017: the architecture every one of the 400 runs uses.
